newsitem.title: USA: Carey holds lead over Hoffa in Teamster vote count.
newsitem.headline: Carey holds lead over Hoffa in Teamster vote count.

text.p: Teamsters Union President Ron Carey held a modest lead over rival James Hoffa in the third day of vote counting Thursday, but major locals that could swing the bitter election had yet to be tallied.

Both campaigns said they expect a close outcome and that at the rate the estimated 511,268 mail-in ballots are being counted by the 500-person staff of a court-appointed election officer, a winner may not be known until the weekend at least.
"We're still crunching numbers, but our view right now is that the final count probably won't happen until Monday," said Hoffa spokesman Richard Leebove.

With about one-third of the ballots tallied by Thursday afternoon, the election officer reported that Carey had 53.3 percent of the vote and was leading Hoffa by 85,830 to 75,171 after counting 211 of the union's 562 locals.
Election Officer Barbara Zack Quindel said that declaring a winner in the race to lead the 1.4 million-member International Brotherhood of Teamsters was not imminent.
"At this time, we're looking at certainly going into Saturday and maybe Sunday," she told a news conference.
Despite Carey's lead, his supporters expect the race to tighten, noting that returns from two-thirds of union's biggest 100 locals had yet to be tallied, including many in Hoffa's Midwest powerbase.
"I think there are more locals that may benefit Hoffa out there than locals that may benefit Carey," said Carey backer Ken Paff of the Detroit-based reform group Teamsters for a Democratic Union.

Hoffa, 55, son the infamous Teamster leader Jimmy Hoffa, is a Detroit labour lawyer who has worked for the past three years for a Teamster joint council that was once headed by his father. His strongholds are considered to be large locals in the Midwest and locals the represent long-haul truckers.

Carey, 60, a former United Parcel Service driver and dissident leader of a New York local, won the Teamster presidency as a reform candidate five years ago in the union's first government-run election open to rank-and-file members. He is considered strongest in the East and among workers at UPS, the union's largest single employer.
The union agreed to government-supervised, rank-and-file elections as part of a 1989 settlement of a federal anti- racketeering suit. Before that top officers were elected by convention delegates.

With the race expected tighten, the outcome may hinge on challenged ballots -- ballots that have been set aside for further review of eligibility and will not be ruled upon or counted unless they are needed to determine a winner.

The election officer reported that there were 11,597 challenged ballots on Thursday afternoon, more than Carey's running margin over Hoffa. Campaign aides for Hoffa expect about 30,000 challenged ballots by the close of vote counting.
Both candidates have positioned themselves for possible post-election challenges.

The Carey campaign Thursday filed a protest with Quindel claiming that a former officer of a 17,000-member local in Chicago collected and mailed at least 115 ballots for other members, an illegal practice under election rules.

Carey counsel Susan Davis said the campaign has asked Quindel to immediately challenge all ballots from that local, whose leaders are backing Hoffa, and eventually to disqualify Hoffa and his running mates from the election.

On Wednesday, the Hoffa camp filed a protest with Quindel. It said some 20,000 sorted, but uncounted ballots were left in a counting room overnight Tuesday after the night shift of ballot counters stopped work, a violation of Quindel's own rules. It also complained that Quindel was deliberately counting Carey-friendly locals first, while skipping Hoffa strongholds.
